cf.title: to_date()/to_timestamp() silently truncate 4+-digit day-of-year input to the first three digits

input.subject: BUG #19650: to_date()/to_timestamp() silently truncate 4+-digit day-of-year input to the first three digits

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal: the patch enforces ranges that the documentation already states, and a second tester confirmed the boundaries in message #3. Two fixable points remain. maintenance-fit-1 asks which branches the fix targets, because input accepted today would start to fail. prior-attempts-1 asks for the rule that checks ID but leaves D unchecked. A committer who knows formatting.c has to decide the back-patch question.

brief.title: Reject out-of-range template fields in to_date() and to_timestamp()
brief.problem: to_date() and to_timestamp() accept some template field values outside their documented ranges and return a date instead of an error. The bug report shows IDDD 999 accepted, and the author lists DDD, IDDD, SSSSS, RM, IW and ID as affected. Users who rely on these functions to validate input get wrong dates silently.
brief.proposed_design: The patch checks each affected field against its documented range when the field is parsed, because a later 0 in TmFromChar means the field was unset. It recovers a minus sign swallowed as a separator before SSSSS, as TZH already does. After RM, it rejects a leftover roman digit so XIII is not read as XII.
user_visible_surface: to_date() and to_timestamp() raise an out-of-range error for IDDD outside 001-371 and DDD outside 001-366.
SSSSS outside 0-86399 now errors, including negative input that unpatched master reads as a positive value.
RM values beyond XII, such as XIII, now error instead of being read as XII.
IW outside 01-53 and ID outside 1-7 now error, including 0.
author_claims: The listed fields accepted values outside their documented domains.
to_date('2024 1000', 'YYYY DDDD') is not a DDD overflow, because DDDD parses as DDD followed by D, which is ignored.
WW 54 and above already errored, and the patch checks week fields uniformly.
brief.thread_state: The author replied to the bug report with a patch. Clemenza Zhang tested it on master, confirmed the boundaries and unchanged in-range ISO normalization, and reported passing tests; no committer has replied.
unclear: The material does not say whether the fix targets master only or is meant for back-branches, where existing queries may start to fail.
The commit message cites bug #19651, but the thread does not say what that report covers.
The bug title claims DDDD truncation, which the author says is not a bug; the material does not say whether the docs should explain how DDDD parses.
No documentation change is listed, so it is unclear whether the docs already describe these ranges and errors.

prior_attempts.title: Correct negative/zero year in to_date/to_timestamp
prior_attempts.quote: But I'm not seeing the argument that hacking at the margins like this moves us forward on either point; what it does do is create another backward-compatibility hazard for any such rewrite.
prior_attempts.reason: Robert Haas and Tom Lane held that input such as '-2-06-01' does not match the format 'YYYY-MM-DD', so its current result is an implementation artifact that should not be redefined. Tom Lane added that the patch adds an error for year zero while still accepting other bad input, and that changes at the margins create another backward-compatibility hazard for a later rewrite of to_date. Both voted to reject, and the author accepted that.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P6 redefined what negative years mean for input that did not match the format. This patch enforces ranges that the documentation already states, but it shares the concern about partial tightening of to_date.

prior_attempts.title: to_date_valid()
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 proposed a separate validating function. This patch tightens to_date and to_timestamp themselves. No reason for P2's outcome is recorded.

objections.title: Behavior change for accepted input needs a stated master-only scope
objections.failure_scenario: An ETL job passes values such as SSSSS '-1', RM 'XIII' or ID '0' to to_timestamp() and gets a timestamp today. If the fix is back-patched, the job starts failing with an out-of-range error after a routine minor upgrade, with no release-note warning it would expect for a major version.
objections.argument: The patch turns input that returns a value today into an error, and Clemenza Zhang's tests in message #3 show master's current result for negative SSSSS. The thread was filed on pgsql-bugs, the CommitFest entry is tagged Bugfix, and neither message #2 nor the commit message says which branches it targets. [P6] records that changes at the margins of to_date create a backward-compatibility hazard. That case redefined results instead of adding errors for documented ranges, so it applies only to the compatibility point.
objections.author_must_show: Is this fix meant for master only, with a release-note entry listing the inputs that now raise errors, or for back-branches too?

critic.reasoning: The commit message and messages #2 and #3 do not name a target branch, and the entry is tagged Bugfix on a pgsql-bugs thread. Message #3 confirms that input accepted today, such as SSSSS -1, would start to fail.

objections.title: Partial range checks leave the reported DDDD case and D unchecked
objections.failure_scenario: A user runs to_date('2024 1000', 'YYYY DDDD') after the patch and still gets 2024-04-09. The patch does not list D among the checked fields, so the trailing 0 is accepted and ignored. The reporter's own example is unchanged, while other bad input now raises errors.
objections.argument: [P6] was rejected partly because it added an error for one bad input while other bad input was still accepted. Tom Lane saw such margin changes as a backward-compatibility hazard for a later rewrite of to_date. This patch adds errors for six fields. Message #2 explains that DDDD parses as DDD plus D, and message #3 confirms the bug's headline cases still return dates. The patch therefore changes behavior for some invalid input but not for the input that started the report.
objections.author_must_show: Why is D left without a 1-7 range check while ID gets one, and what rule decides which invalid inputs this patch rejects?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 explains how DDDD parses but gives no rule for leaving D unchecked while ID gets a 1-7 check. [P6] is weak support, because its input did not match the format, while these fields have documented ranges.

refuted.title: Stricter parsing breaks queries that returned dates; target branch not stated
refuted.failure_scenario: An ETL job calls to_timestamp() with SSSSS on feeds where '-1' or '86400' appear, or to_date() with IW 00 or RM XIII. It gets a date today. After a minor upgrade that carries this fix, the load aborts with an out-of-range error, and the operator finds out when the nightly job fails.
refuted.argument: The patch turns accepted input into errors for six fields, so it changes the user-facing contract. The commit message and messages #2 and #3 do not say whether the fix targets master only. The documented ranges support calling this a bug fix, but [P6] shows committers treat margin changes to to_date as a compatibility hazard. No documentation or release-note hunk tells users which inputs now fail.
refuted.author_must_show: Is this fix meant for master only, and will the release notes list the newly rejected inputs, such as negative SSSSS and IW 00?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which states the same branch-target question and limits its use of [P6] more carefully. The missing release-note hunk is not a gap, because committers write release notes at release time.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Input that returns a date today, such as SSSSS -1 or RM XIII, raises an error after the patch, and no target branch is named.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch tightens six fields in formatting.c and leaves D unchecked, so the set of rejected input stays uneven.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Is this fix meant for master only, or for back-branches too, where queries that return a date today would start to fail?
Why does D get no 1-7 range check while ID gets one, and what rule decides which invalid inputs the patch rejects?
What does bug #19651, cited in the commit message, report, and which part of the patch fixes it?
Should the documentation say that DDDD parses as DDD followed by D, since the reporter's headline cases still return dates?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the to_char/to_date parser in formatting.c and the project's back-patch policy for stricter input checks.
committability.liability: The owner signs for every query that starts to fail on the six fields, including immutable wrappers used in indexes or CHECK constraints. If back-patched, that covers all supported branches.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered the bug report with a patch the same day and opened the CommitFest entry; no later reply is visible.

priority.reason: The patch is 9.1 KB in one source file plus regression tests, and it fixes silent wrong dates for documented ranges. Few users pass out-of-range values in these six fields, but those who do get wrong dates today.

provisional_note: The code was not read. The SSSSS minus-sign recovery and the RM leftover-digit check could change results for in-range input with unusual separators, and only the code can show that.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Refactor compile-time assertion checks for C/C++
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch merged the fallback implementations of StaticAssertStmt, StaticAssertExpr and StaticAssertDecl in c.h so that C and C++ share one set. The goal was fewer separate code paths for compile-time assertions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch was committed as v3 and then reverted. The shared fallback broke StaticAssertExpr and StaticAssertStmt in C++: older g++ (4.4.7) rejects a struct defined inside sizeof, and MSVC 2015 rejected the do{} form that would fix it. Fixing both would need about four implementations, so the refactoring no longer reduced code.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It's looking like we're going to end up with four or so
implementations no matter what, so it's getting hard to see any
real benefit.

precedents_retrieved.title: invalid bit/varbit input causes the log file to be unreadable
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changed the bit_in and varbit_in error messages so they no longer print an invalid input byte with %c, because that byte can make a CSV log invalid UTF8 and unreadable through file_fdw. The goal was a log file that decodes correctly after bad bit or varbit input.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane doubted the premise, because Postgres does not guarantee that the log file is valid in any one encoding. He also found the patch less user-friendly and incomplete, since many other %c error messages have the same problem. He wrote and pushed his own patch, which prints one whole valid character with pg_mblen() across the backend, so the original entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Even granting the premise, the proposed patch seems like a significant
decrease in user-friendliness for typical cases.  I'd rather see us
make an effort to print one valid-per-the-DB-encoding character.

precedents_retrieved.title: This adds a new GUC parameter that automatically rolls back prepared transactions that have remained unresolved beyond the configured timeout. The cleanup is performed by the checkpointer process.
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andrey Borodin, Artur Zakirov, Greg Sabino Mullane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a GUC, prepared_orphaned_transaction_timeout, that makes the checkpointer roll back prepared transactions older than the timeout. It is disabled by default (0) and is modelled on idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and similar timeouts.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers said a silent rollback breaks the 2PC protocol: after all participants PREPARE, COMMIT must succeed on a healthy database, and only the transaction manager knows whether a dangling prepared transaction should be committed or rolled back. An orphaned prepared transaction signals a serious malfunction that needs monitoring, and a DBA who wants a timeout can use a cron job. Users who enable 2PC are expected to have their own monitoring and handling.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Silent rollback in any scenario I can imagine is a disaster.

precedents_retrieved.title: Correct negative/zero year in to_date/to_timestamp
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes to_date and to_timestamp so that a negative year in the input (YYYY) maps to the same BC year, instead of one year earlier, and year 0 raises an error. It also makes a negative year or century override the era indicator.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas and Tom Lane held that input such as '-2-06-01' does not match the format 'YYYY-MM-DD', so its current result is an implementation artifact that should not be redefined. Tom Lane added that the patch adds an error for year zero while still accepting other bad input, and that changes at the margins create another backward-compatibility hazard for a later rewrite of to_date. Both voted to reject, and the author accepted that.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But I'm not seeing the argument that hacking at the margins
like this moves us forward on either point; what it does do is create
another backward-compatibility hazard for any such rewrite.

precedents_retrieved.title: Free list same_input_transnos in preprocess_aggref
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a list_free() call in preprocess_aggref() to release the same_input_transnos list after find_compatible_trans() returns. The goal was to stop leaking one small list per aggregate during planning, as find_compatible_agg() already frees the list in one path.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane asked for a case where the change makes a measurable difference, then instrumented the code himself. In the core regression tests the list was almost always empty and never longer than two elements, so the saving is negligible next to the many other small allocations the planner leaks. The author agreed and withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The two one-element lists are absolutely, completely negligible in the context of planning any nontrivial statement.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add generate_series(date,date,[step])
precedents_retrieved.objectors: David Steele, Tom Lane, Robert Haas
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds generate_series(date, date) and generate_series(date, date, integer), which return dates with a step in days. It returns an empty set when either endpoint is infinite.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Adding generate_series(date, date, integer) changes how the parser resolves existing calls such as generate_series('01-01-2000'::date, '01-04-2000'::date, '7 days'). Those calls now pick the integer step and fail, where before they resolved to the timestamptz version. A rename to generate_dates() removed the main benefit for supporters, and David Steele and Tom Lane moved to -1. The author withdrew the patch, and Robert Haas judged a generate_series(date, date, interval) variant too different to redesign that late in the commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: So if you had written such a call with an interval literal and didn't bother to cast the literal, your code would break.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix for PL/Python slow input arrays traversal issue
precedents_retrieved.summary: PL/Python converted input arrays by calling array_ref for each element, which costs O(N^2) for arrays with nulls or variable-size elements. The patch walks the array once and keeps the offset of the last element, as array_out does.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was closed as a duplicate because the same change is part of another patch, commitfest entry 697. The thread contains no objection to the fix itself.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Yes, this should be closed as it is contained in https://commitfest.postgresql.org/10/697/

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Reject concurrent sequence refreshes".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Reject concurrent sequence refreshes".
Reverted commit(s): Reject concurrent sequence refreshes.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit f38afa4abb04e85530c94b88daf11c089375daca.

That commit fixed a race that could leave stale sequence values on the
subscriber after 'ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... REFRESH SEQUENCES'. It did so by
raising an ERROR during 'ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... REFRESH SEQUENCES'
whenever a sequence synchronization worker was already running for the
subscription.

That approach caused intermittent buildfarm failures, because the existing
tests did not ensure the sequencesync worker had stopped before executing
'ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... REFRESH SEQUENCES'. While discussing how to fix
the tests, we concluded that blocking the command while a sequencesync
worker is running is inconvenient for users. So we will fix the original
race differently in a follow-up commit.

roaster_notes.note: One objection raised. [P1] (WW-D parsing) is a different idea and is not listed.
Apart from the back-branch question, the change matches documented ranges and adds no syntax, GUC or dump surface.

The patch changes only how to_date() and to_timestamp() parse text input in formatting.c. It changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol message or exported struct, so pg_upgrade, standbys and subscribers are not affected. One edge case remains, and it is a compatibility question for back-branches. A user who wraps these functions in an immutable function for an index, generated column or CHECK constraint may hit new errors on reindex or restore. The same holds for any stricter input check, and the backpatch angle should weigh it.

The patch only makes to_date() and to_timestamp() reject out-of-range template field values, so it has no privilege, exposure, or denial-of-service aspect. It adds no new privilege, object, setting, or code path that an unprivileged user could use to see or do more than before, and the error text echoes only the caller's own input.

From the maintenance and fit angle the design is small and fits core. It adds range checks in formatting.c of the kind that already exist for DDD 367 and WW 54, and the SSSSS sign recovery copies TZH. It has no hot-path cost outside these functions, adds no new API or dependency, and creates no state that needs cleanup. Only the branch scope stands as an objection.

No objection from this angle. Postgres has no other function, option or extension that range-checks DDD, IDDD, SSSSS, RM, IW or ID in to_date() and to_timestamp() templates. The patch adds checks inside the existing parser and does not add a second mechanism. The margin-change concern in [P6] is about compatibility, which another panel member covers.

No demand objection. The patch fixes cases where to_date() and to_timestamp() return a wrong date silently instead of the documented error. A user report shows one such case (IDDD 999), and a second tester confirmed the others in message #3. Fixing documented behaviour does not need proof of a large user group. The cost is a possible break for queries that depend on the lenient parsing, and [P6] shows committers weighing that kind of risk. That question belongs to the compatibility angle, not to demand.
